chapters.title: Force Is An Interaction
chapters.learningOutcome: Identify the two objects in a force interaction and distinguish contact from non-contact forces.

narration.title: Watch the motion
narration.text: Watch the two pilots on the glide track. At first, both are still. Now watch their hands. Their palms press, and both platforms begin to move apart. The motion is our first clue. Which two objects are interacting?

narration.title: A force needs two
narration.text: A force is a push or pull during an interaction. The blue pilot pushes on the orange pilot. At the same moment, the orange pilot pushes on the blue pilot. One interaction produces two forces, acting on two different objects.

narration.title: Name both objects
narration.text: Follow each arrow to the object receiving the push. Blue on orange belongs with the orange pilot. Orange on blue belongs with the blue pilot. The arrows are equal in length and point in opposite directions. One interaction; two force arrows.

narration.title: Motion is evidence
narration.text: Compare the evidence before and after contact. Before the push, both platforms are still. Afterwards, they move apart. The change is motion. We do not see a force floating through the air; we identify the interaction and measure what changes.

narration.title: The push has ended
narration.text: Here is an idea worth testing: perhaps the push travels inside each pilot. Check the sequence. While their palms touch, the contact-force arrows are present. When their hands separate, those arrows disappear. The platforms keep gliding, but that contact push has ended.

narration.title: Push or pull
narration.text: Contact forces can push or pull. In the first bay, the robot's padded hand pushes the cart. In the second, the robot pulls the trolley through a taut cable. In both cases, name the pair. One object alone cannot describe an interaction.

narration.title: No touch required
narration.text: Now focus on the gap between the magnets. They do not touch, yet both carts can begin to move. That is evidence of a non-contact interaction. Gravity is another example: Earth pulls objects towards it without making surface contact.

narration.title: Contact or non-contact
narration.text: Use two questions to classify an interaction. First: which two objects are involved? Second: do they touch? A robot hand on a cart is contact. Magnet on magnet is non-contact. Earth pulling an object is non-contact. Strength does not choose the label; touching does.

narration.title: Test one change
narration.text: For a fair comparison, keep the cart, track, and starting line the same. Change only the size of the push, then measure the distance travelled in the same time. If several conditions change together, the evidence cannot tell us which change mattered.

narration.title: Repair the explanation
narration.text: Return to the pilots. Their platforms are still moving after their hands separate. Does that mean a push is stored inside them? No. The contact interaction happened first and changed their motion. After contact ends, the new motion can continue while other forces still act.

narration.title: Predict the evidence
narration.text: Make a prediction before the magnet trial runs. Which observations would support a non-contact interaction? Take three quiet seconds to decide. Now check: the gap remains visible, both carts change motion, and no hand touches either cart. Those observations support the claim.

narration.title: Your physics move
narration.text: Use this physicist's routine whenever you investigate a force. Name both objects. Decide whether they touch. Then use a change in motion as evidence. A force is not hidden material carried by one object. A force belongs to an interaction between objects.

tests.prompt: Two skaters press palms and move apart. Which statement names the interaction most completely?
options: Skater A pushes skater B, and skater B pushes skater A
The floor gives both skaters stored motion
tests.feedback: A force interaction involves two objects. Each skater pushes on the other during contact.

tests.prompt: A foot kicks a still ball. Which object pair belongs in the contact-force explanation?
tests.feedback: The foot and ball touch during the kick, so they are the relevant interaction pair.

tests.prompt: Skater A is on the left and pushes Skater B to the right. Which way should the arrow labelled 'A on B' point?
tests.feedback: The arrow shows the direction of the force on B, so it points to the right.

tests.prompt: A hand pulls a trolley left with a rope. Which arrow best represents 'rope on trolley'?
options: An arrow left from the trolley
An arrow right from the trolley
An arrow down from the rope
No arrow because pulling is not a force
tests.feedback: The rope pulls the trolley left, so the force arrow on the trolley points left.

tests.prompt: Both skaters are still before their palms meet and moving apart afterwards. What is the strongest evidence that forces acted?
options: Their motion changed after the contact
tests.feedback: A change from still to moving is observable evidence that forces affected the skaters' motion.

tests.prompt: A cart is still, then speeds up while a hand pushes it. Which two observations form useful before-and-after evidence?
options: Still before and speeding up during the push
tests.feedback: Comparing motion before and during the push links the interaction to a visible change.

tests.prompt: The skaters' hands separate, but they continue gliding. What happened to the hand-to-hand push?
tests.feedback: The hand-to-hand contact force ends when the hands separate; continuing motion does not mean the push is stored.

tests.prompt: A foot leaves a kicked ball. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: The foot's push continues inside the ball
The foot-ball force ended when contact ended
No force acted at any time
The ball now creates its own kick
tests.feedback: The foot's contact force acts during contact and ends when the foot leaves the ball.

tests.prompt: Two magnet carts begin still with a visible gap and then move apart. Which conclusion fits the evidence?
options: A contact push acted through the track
A non-contact magnetic interaction changed their motion
The carts stored force before the test
No force acted because they did not touch
tests.feedback: The gap remains visible while motion changes, supporting a non-contact magnetic interaction.

tests.prompt: A book falls after being released. Which interaction can act without contact between the book and the ground?
tests.feedback: Earth's gravitational pull on the book is a non-contact interaction.

tests.prompt: A rope moves a trolley towards a child. Which description is complete?
options: The rope pulls on the trolley during contact
The child stores force in the trolley
Gravity pulls the trolley towards the child
tests.feedback: The rope and trolley interact through contact, and the rope pulls the trolley.

tests.prompt: A hand moves a cart away from the child. Which words best describe the interaction?
tests.feedback: The hand is in contact with the cart and pushes it away.

tests.prompt: A student compares a gentle and strong push. Which plan gives the clearest evidence?
options: Change the cart, surface and push together
Use the same cart and surface, change only the push, and measure distance
Use two carts and guess which moved faster
Change only the surface and call it a push test
tests.feedback: Keeping the cart and surface the same isolates the push as the changed variable.

tests.prompt: Two carts travel different distances, but one ran on carpet and one on tile. Why can this test not compare push strength fairly?
options: A strong push never changes motion
tests.feedback: Changing the surface as well as the push creates two possible causes for the distance difference.

tests.prompt: Which claim contains the 'force is stored inside' misconception?
options: A hand pushes a cart during contact
A magnet can push another magnet across a gap
The kick's force rides inside the ball after contact
Earth pulls on a falling book
tests.feedback: A force is an interaction; the foot-ball contact force does not ride inside the ball.

tests.prompt: A student says, 'No force can act unless objects touch.' Which observation best challenges the claim?
tests.feedback: The visible gap and changing motion show that a magnetic force can act without contact.

tests.prompt: A ball changes from still to moving when kicked. Which reasoning chain is strongest?
options: The ball moved, so it must contain force
Foot and ball touched; the foot pushed the ball; the ball's motion changed
The goal pulled the ball forwards
The ball moved because moving is natural
tests.feedback: The answer names the interacting objects, the push and the observed change in motion.

tests.prompt: Two magnets do not touch, yet one cart starts moving. Which three-part explanation is best?
options: There was a gap; magnetic interaction acted; motion changed
The cart had wheels; wheels contain force; motion appeared
The bench pushed sideways; the magnet did nothing
tests.feedback: The explanation links the visible gap, a non-contact interaction and the change in motion.

tests.prompt: A diagram shows only one arrow labelled 'push' between two skaters. What is the most useful improvement?
options: Add the two object names and show the matching opposite interaction
Remove all arrows because forces are invisible
tests.feedback: Object-pair labels and the matching interaction make the force model precise.

tests.prompt: Which final explanation uses claim and evidence most effectively?
options: A force happened because I think so
The magnets repelled because they are blue
A non-contact magnetic push acted because the carts moved apart while a gap remained
The carts moved because the track was long
tests.feedback: The claim names the force type and the evidence identifies the visible gap and motion change.

chapters.title: Motion Tells The Story
chapters.learningOutcome: Use before-and-after evidence to explain changes in motion.

narration.title: Three tracks, one mystery
narration.text: Three identical balls. Three different tracks. Each ball gets the same launch. Tile, short grass, or thick carpet: which ball will travel furthest before it stops? Make your prediction, then watch for evidence.

narration.title: Run the comparison
narration.text: All three begin still. The same launcher setting sends each ball across a smooth launch strip. A timing gate confirms the same entry speed before each test surface. Now the launcher is clear. Tile gives the longest stopping distance. Grass is shorter. Carpet is shortest.

narration.title: Name the motion changes
narration.text: Motion can tell several stories. Still to moving means start. More distance in the same time means speed up. Less distance each moment means slow down. No new distance means stop. A new path means change direction.

narration.title: Before and after evidence
narration.text: A physicist compares before and after. Before the launch, the carpet ball is still. Just after contact, it is moving. Later, its gaps become smaller. Finally, its position no longer changes. That sequence is measurable evidence.

narration.title: The kick has ended
narration.text: Look closely at the contact. While the launcher touches the ball, launcher on ball is a forward push. Once the launcher separates, that contact force ends. The ball can still be moving even though the kick is over.

narration.title: What slows the ball?
narration.text: The moving ball still interacts with its surroundings. The surface touches the ball. In this carpet model, friction and carpet deformation produce a backward surface resistance. The greater slowing effect gives a shorter stopping distance.

narration.title: Build a fair test
narration.text: To compare surfaces fairly, keep the ball, entry speed, and start line the same. Change only the surface. Measure from the surface start to the resting ball. Repeat each run, because one surprising run may not represent the pattern.

narration.title: Read the data
narration.text: Check all three runs before the averages. Tile measures three hundred and thirty-five, three hundred and forty-five, and three hundred and forty centimetres: average three hundred and forty. Grass averages two hundred and twenty. Carpet averages one hundred and ten. The graph and tracks show the same pattern.

narration.title: Test the tempting idea
narration.text: A tempting explanation says the kick force rides inside the ball and slowly runs out. But the contact arrow ended when the launcher separated. The remaining evidence shows a ball moving while surface friction acts against that motion. The kick is not stored inside.

narration.title: Direction is evidence too
narration.text: A force can change direction as well as speed. A rolling ball meets an angled bumper. The bumper-on-ball force points away from the bumper surface. That force changes the ball's motion into a new path: straight in, diagonal out.

narration.title: Make a prediction
narration.text: Suppose we replace thick carpet with a more deformable, higher-resistance rubber mat while everything else stays the same. Predict the stopping distance. Would it be longer than tile, between tile and carpet, or shorter than carpet? Use the model, then test it. Our testable prediction is shorter than carpet.

narration.title: Your evidence routine
narration.text: Use this motion routine. Compare before and after. Name the motion change. Name the interacting objects. Then connect the force to visible evidence. The ball does not carry a used-up kick. Motion changes because objects are interacting now, or interacted earlier while other forces continue to act.

tests.prompt: A ball is still, then rolls after a launcher touches it. Which motion change occurred?
tests.feedback: The before-and-after evidence changes from still to moving, so the ball started.

tests.prompt: A cart keeps the same speed, hits a bumper, then moves diagonally. What changed?
tests.feedback: The path before and after contact shows a change in direction.

tests.prompt: Position dots become closer together each second. What does that show?
tests.feedback: Smaller distances in equal times show that the object is slowing down.

tests.prompt: Position dots become farther apart each second. Which conclusion fits?
tests.feedback: Larger distances in equal time intervals show increasing speed.

tests.prompt: When does the launcher's contact force on the ball end?
tests.feedback: The launcher-on-ball contact force ends when contact ends.

tests.prompt: A foot leaves a kicked ball, but the ball keeps moving. Which statement is accurate?
options: The foot-ball push ended at separation
The ball now has no interactions
tests.feedback: Continuing motion does not mean the earlier contact force is stored.

tests.prompt: In this carpet model, a ball rolls right while carpet deforms beneath it. Which arrow represents the net surface resistance?
options: A left arrow on the ball
A right arrow on the ball
A downward arrow on the start gate
A forward launcher arrow after separation
tests.feedback: For this model, the friction-and-deformation effect is represented by a backward surface-resistance arrow.

tests.prompt: Which two objects form the surface interaction that slows a ball on grass?
tests.feedback: The touching ball and grass are the relevant surface interaction pair.

tests.prompt: Same ball and entry speed: tile 340 cm, grass 220 cm, carpet 110 cm. Which stops after the shortest distance?
options: The data shows only stopping time
tests.feedback: The carpet run has the shortest measured stopping distance.

tests.prompt: Which observation best supports a greater slowing effect on carpet than tile?
options: The ball stops after a shorter distance on carpet
The carpet trial begins at a different speed
The tile trial runs for less time
The carpet ball has greater mass
tests.feedback: With entry speed and ball controlled, stopping distance is relevant motion evidence.

tests.prompt: Which plan fairly compares tile and carpet?
options: Same ball and launch; change only surface; repeat and measure
tests.feedback: A fair surface test holds the ball, launch and start constant, then repeats measurements.

tests.prompt: One trial uses a small ball entering tile at 1 m/s and a large ball entering carpet at 2 m/s. Why is the comparison weak?
options: Ball and entry speed both changed
Stopping distance is the controlled variable
tests.feedback: Changing ball and entry speed prevents a clear conclusion about the surface.

tests.prompt: Which order matches the measured stopping distances from longest to shortest?
tests.feedback: The data is tile 340 cm, grass 220 cm, carpet 110 cm.

tests.prompt: Tile runs measure 335, 345 and 340 cm. Why is 340 cm a useful summary?
options: It is the average of the repeated runs
It proves every future run is 340
tests.feedback: The average summarises the three close repeated measurements without claiming every run is identical.

tests.prompt: Which sentence contains the stored-kick misconception?
options: The kick ended when contact ended
Surface friction acts while the ball rolls
Kick force rides inside the ball and runs out
The ball's motion can be measured
tests.feedback: A force belongs to an interaction; the kick does not ride inside the ball.

tests.prompt: Which evidence most directly challenges 'the kick stays inside the ball'?
options: The contact arrow disappears at separation while the ball keeps moving
tests.feedback: The force arrow ends with contact, separating the earlier push from later motion.

tests.prompt: A ball hits an angled bumper and turns. Which force arrow is most defensible?
options: Bumper on ball pointing away from the bumper surface
A motion arrow labelled force along the old path
Launcher on ball after contact has ended
A friction arrow pointing through the bumper
tests.feedback: The bumper's contact force points away from its surface and changes the ball's velocity.

tests.prompt: Which before-and-after evidence best shows a direction change?
options: Straight path in, diagonal path out
Blue ball in, blue ball out
tests.feedback: A changed path is direct evidence of changed direction.

tests.prompt: Which explanation best uses claim and evidence?
options: Carpet slowed the ball more because its stopping distance was shortest in repeated fair runs
Carpet wins because it looks thick
The kick ran out first on carpet
tests.feedback: The explanation links a force claim to repeated stopping-distance evidence.

tests.prompt: A higher-resistance mat gives repeated stopping distances shorter than carpet at the same entry speed. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The mat produced a greater slowing effect in this fair test
All rubber mats always stop every object fastest
The launcher force ran out inside the ball
The shorter distance proves the ball entered more slowly
tests.feedback: The claim stays within the fair test and links the measured pattern to the changed surface.

chapters.title: Push, Pull And Support
chapters.learningOutcome: Model applied and support forces with a comparison meter.

narration.title: The quiet force mystery
narration.text: This book is not moving, but the foam beneath it is squashed. Is the foam doing nothing? Watch the contact patch. The book presses down, and the foam changes shape. What might the foam be doing to the book?

narration.title: Name both objects
narration.text: The book and foam interact through contact. Book on foam pushes down; foam on book pushes up. Those arrows act on different objects. To explain the resting book, follow forces on the book: Earth on book points down, while foam on book support points up.

narration.title: Still can have forces
narration.text: The book remains still while the foam is supporting it. Remove the foam, and the book begins to fall. Put the support back, and the book can rest again. Stillness is not proof that no forces act.

narration.title: Change the load
narration.text: Add a second identical book. The foam squashes further. To support the resting stack, the foam's upward push is greater than it was for one book. A longer arrow shows greater force within this comparison.

narration.title: Applied pushes
narration.text: Now move to the cart. A robot hand touches the cart and pushes to the right. Hand on cart is an applied force. The arrow begins on the cart and points in the direction of the push.

narration.title: Applied pulls
narration.text: A rubber band can pull the same cart. The band stretches towards the robot. Rubber band on cart points towards the robot too. Push and pull describe the direction of the applied interaction; neither is material stored in the cart.

narration.title: Build a comparison meter
narration.text: We can use band stretch as a comparison meter. Mark the resting length as zero centimetres. Then read how many centimetres the band stretches while pulling. More stretch means a greater pull in this investigation. These are relative readings, not Newtons.

narration.title: Run a fair pull test
narration.text: Keep the cart, surface, and start line the same. First, hold a two-centimetre stretch for one second. Reset. Then hold a four-centimetre stretch for one second. Change only the stretch reading and measure the distance after the same time.

narration.title: Read the result
narration.text: At two centimetres, the cart travels eighty centimetres. At four centimetres, it travels one hundred and fifty centimetres. The larger stretch reading goes with the larger change in motion in this test. The data supports a stronger-pull explanation.

narration.title: Repair the silent-table idea
narration.text: Now test the claim: a table does nothing because it does not move. Place the foam and book on the table. The contact patch changes shape, and the book rests instead of passing through. The surface is part of the interaction.

narration.title: Choose the correct model
narration.text: Which model fits the forces acting on a book resting on foam? One downward Earth-on-book arrow only? No arrows because it is still? Or Earth on book down paired with foam on book support up? Choose, then check the contact evidence.

narration.title: Your force-model routine
narration.text: Use this routine. Name both objects. Mark the contact. Draw the force on the receiving object. Point the arrow in the force direction. When comparing pulls, use the same meter and a fair test. Even a still surface can push. Evidence makes that invisible interaction understandable.

tests.prompt: A book rests on squashed foam. Which objects form the support interaction?
tests.feedback: The touching book and foam are the interaction pair.

tests.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the book-foam interaction pair?
options: Book pushes foam down and foam pushes book up
Both arrows act on the book
Only the book exerts a force
Earth and table are the contact pair
tests.feedback: The two contact forces act on different receivers: one on foam and one on book.

tests.prompt: Which way should the arrow labelled 'foam on book' point?
tests.feedback: The foam's support force on the book points upward.

tests.prompt: Where should a support-force arrow be anchored in the book-and-foam model?
tests.feedback: A force arrow is drawn on the object receiving the force.

tests.prompt: A book is still on a table. Which forces-on-book model is best?
options: Earth on book down and table on book up
No forces because it is still
Book on table down is the only force on the book
tests.feedback: The book can remain still while Earth pulls down and the table supports it upward.

tests.prompt: Which observation challenges 'the foam does nothing'?
options: The foam compresses where the book touches
tests.feedback: Visible compression is evidence that the foam is part of the contact interaction.

tests.prompt: A second identical book is added and the foam compresses further. What should happen to the support arrow in this comparison?
tests.feedback: For the resting stack, greater compression is modelled with a greater upward support force.

tests.prompt: What does a longer upward support arrow mean within the one-book versus two-book scene?
options: Greater support force in this comparison
The arrow acts on the foam
tests.feedback: Within the same comparison, arrow length represents relative force strength on the receiving stack.

tests.prompt: A robot hand pushes a cart right. Which arrow is correct?
options: Cart on hand pointing right from empty space
No arrow because the cart moves
tests.feedback: The applied force on the receiving cart points in the push direction.

tests.prompt: Which two objects belong in the applied-push label?
tests.feedback: The hand and cart touch during the applied push.

tests.prompt: A stretched rubber band pulls a cart towards a robot. Which way does 'band on cart' point?
tests.feedback: The pull on the cart points along the stretched band towards the robot.

tests.prompt: Which sentence correctly separates pull from later motion?
options: The stretched band pulls during contact; that pull ends when the band disconnects
The cart carries the band's pull after disconnection
The pull becomes the cart's speed
The cart pulls itself after release
tests.feedback: A pull is an interaction; later motion is not stored pull material.

tests.prompt: In this comparison meter, what does 4 cm of stretch mean compared with 2 cm?
options: A greater pull in this investigation
The cart is twice as heavy
tests.feedback: More stretch represents a greater relative pull here; centimetres are not Newtons.

tests.prompt: Why must the meter be labelled 'relative comparison'?
options: Centimetres measure stretch, not a standard force unit
tests.feedback: The ruler measures band stretch as a proxy for comparing pulls, not force in Newtons.

tests.prompt: Which plan fairly compares 2 cm and 4 cm stretches?
options: Same cart, surface, start and time; change only stretch
tests.feedback: Holding other conditions constant isolates the stretch reading.

tests.prompt: Why is a 2 cm pull for one second versus a 4 cm pull for three seconds unfair?
tests.feedback: Changing both stretch and pull time creates two possible causes.

tests.prompt: The cart travels 80 cm at 2 cm stretch and 150 cm at 4 cm stretch. What does the data support?
options: The larger stretch went with a larger motion change
tests.feedback: The fair-test data links the larger relative pull with greater distance in the same time.

tests.prompt: Which graph matches the fair pull test?
options: A 150 cm bar for 4 cm stretch and 80 cm bar for 2 cm
A 150 cm bar for 2 cm and 80 cm for 4 cm
Equal bars because the same cart was used
Bars of stretch rather than measured cart distance
tests.feedback: The 4 cm trial produced the greater measured cart distance.

tests.prompt: Which is the strongest forces-on-book model for a book resting on foam?
options: Earth on book down and foam on book up, both anchored to the book
Book on foam down and foam on book up as if both act on the book
No arrows because the book is still
tests.feedback: A forces-on-one-object model keeps both arrows on the receiving book and names both source objects.

tests.prompt: Which explanation fully names the pair, direction and evidence?
options: Foam pushes upward on the book; the compressed contact patch and resting book support that model
The foam has force because it is blue
The book pushes down, so that is the only force on the book
The table is still, so no upward interaction exists
tests.feedback: The answer identifies source and receiver, upward direction, and relevant contact evidence.

chapters.title: Magnets Push And Pull
chapters.learningOutcome: Predict magnetic attraction and repulsion using evidence.

chapters.learningOutcome: Use several qualitative arrows to predict motion.

chapters.learningOutcome: Investigate how shape changes air resistance.

chapters.learningOutcome: Explain how ramps and levers trade force for distance.

chapters.title: The Broken Experiment
chapters.learningOutcome: Diagnose unfair tests and strengthen conclusions.
